title: Operational amplifiers
blurb: Read the inverting op-amp in figure E7-3, calculate its gain and output, and explain what real op-amps do differently from ideal ones.

E7G01.why: The output stage is built to drive a load: output impedance is **very low**.
E7G01.trap: Very high is the input side, where the op-amp must not load the source.

E7G02.why: A capacitor's reactance falls with frequency, so across RF it cuts the feedback resistance and the gain at high frequencies: **low-pass**.
E7G02.trap: High-pass needs the capacitor in series with the input.

E7G03.why: The inputs draw almost no current, so input impedance is **very high**.
E7G03.trap: Low input impedance would load the source down.

E7G04.why: Offset voltage is the **differential input needed to bring the open-loop output to zero**: the amplifier's built-in imbalance.
E7G04.trap: It is an input-side imbalance, not an output-minus-input difference.

E7G05.why: High gain and high Q make a filter ring and become unstable, so **restrict both gain and Q**.
E7G05.trap: Raising either one pushes the filter toward ringing.

E7G06.why: Open-loop gain falls with frequency. **Gain-bandwidth** is the frequency where it has fallen to one.
E7G06.trap: It isn't a filter's maximum or cutoff frequency.

E7G07.trap: R1 ÷ RF = 0.21 is upside down. 4700 multiplies instead of dividing.

E7G08.why: An **ideal** op-amp has the same gain at all frequencies. Real ones lose gain as frequency rises.
E7G08.trap: Falling gain describes real op-amps, not the ideal one.

E7G09.trap: Skipping the minus sign gives +2.3 V. The inverting input flips polarity.

E7G12.why: An op-amp is a high-gain, direct-coupled **differential** amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance.
